reason: Multiple independent sources corroborate Phobos's orbital decay, rubble-pile structure, and future destruction into a ring.
story: Mars harbors a doomed companion. Orbiting just 3,700 miles above the Martian surface—closer than any other moon in the solar system—Phobos circles Mars in under eight hours, moving so quickly that it rises in the west and sets in the east. But its extreme proximity is a death sentence. Mars's relentless gravity is dragging Phobos inward by approximately two meters every century. Phobos is not solid rock; it is a porous rubble pile barely bound by a thin outer layer. The mysterious parallel grooves gouged across its battered surface are actually structural stretch marks, revealing that the moon is already tearing apart under immense tidal stresses. In 20 to 50 million years, gravity will cross the ultimate threshold. Mars will violently rip Phobos apart, shredding the moon into a dense planetary ring system that will circle the Red Planet for up to 100 million years.
angle: The mysterious grooves carved across Mars's largest moon are gravitational stretch marks, proving the moon is actively being torn apart into a future ring.

claims.claim: Phobos was discovered in 1877 by American astronomer Asaph Hall.
Phobos is the larger of the two natural moons of Mars.
Phobos orbits roughly 6,000 kilometers (3,700 miles) above the Martian surface.
Phobos orbits closer to its host planet than any other known natural satellite in the Solar System.
Phobos completes an entire orbit around Mars in approximately 7 hours and 39 minutes.
Because Phobos orbits faster than Mars rotates, it appears to rise in the west and set in the east.
From the surface of Mars, Phobos crosses the sky in four hours and 15 minutes or less.
Phobos is one of the darkest and least reflective bodies in the Solar System.
Surface temperatures on Phobos swing from roughly −4 °C (25 °F) in sunlight down to −112 °C (−170 °F) in shadow.
Stickney crater is the dominant impact feature on Phobos.
The giant collision that created Stickney crater was powerful enough that it came close to completely shattering Phobos.
Phobos is not a solid rock, but rather a porous rubble pile held together by an outer crust or layer.
Gravitational tidal forces from Mars are steadily decelerating Phobos and causing its orbit to spiral inward.
Phobos's orbital altitude is decaying at a rate of approximately 1.8 to 2 meters per century.
The prominent grooves across Phobos's surface are interpreted as structural failure fractures or stretch marks caused by tidal stresses.
Phobos is predicted to break up or collide with Mars in roughly 20 to 50 million years.
When tidal forces tear Phobos apart, the dispersed debris will form a planetary ring around Mars.
The predicted Martian ring formed from the breakup of Phobos is expected to persist for 1 million to 100 million years.
JAXA is preparing the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission to collect and return samples from Phobos.

disputed: Origin of Phobos's grooves: Some researchers suggest they were caused by rolling boulders from the Stickney impact or ejecta from impacts on Mars, while others model them as tidal stress fractures. The script should attribute tidal stretch marks as the latest modeling while acknowledging competing impact ejecta theories.

Origin of the moons: Competing models propose Phobos is a captured asteroid, debris from a giant impact on Mars, or fragments of a destroyed parent moon. The script should present the origin as an ongoing scientific mystery.

Hollow artificial satellite theory: A mid-20th-century proposal by Iosif Shklovsky suggested Phobos was a hollow artificial shell. The script should clearly present this as a debunked historical hypothesis caused by erroneous early orbital tracking and an April Fool's hoax.
